The brown antechinus (Antechinus stuartii) is a small dasyurid marsupial known for its semelparous reproductive strategy, a life-history pattern that imposes severe physiological costs on males. Neonates weigh only 0.0164 grams [Wwb = 0.0164 grams] at parturition, a remarkably diminutive size reflective of the altricial state typical of marsupial newborns. These tiny young, born after a brief gestation period, must immediately crawl to the teat within the mother's pouch, where they will remain attached for an extended period of lactation. The energetic demands of this strategy are substantial; field metabolic measurements indicate that the species exhibits a maximum basal metabolic rate of 36.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a body temperature of 35.9 °C [T = 35.9 °C]. This elevated metabolic performance is thought to support the intense activity levels required for foraging and male competition during the brief, synchronous mating season. The strict seasonality of reproduction in this species is one of its most distinctive characteristics, with all adult males dying shortly after the rut.

Females of this species give birth to a single litter each year, with litter sizes typically comprising seven pups [N_R_i = litter sizes typically comprising seven pups]. This restricted annual reproductive output, combined with the complete post-mating mortality of males, places a premium on successful rearing by the mother. During the period of lactation, the female's resources are heavily taxed, and the offspring undergo a considerable period of dependency within the pouch. Weaning, the point at which the young become nutritionally independent from the mother and transition to solid food, occurs at 106 days after birth [tx = 106 days after birth], a duration that coincides with the warmer austral summer months when insect prey is abundant at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. At this milestone, the young animals have achieved a wet weight of approximately 16 grams [Wwx = approximately 16 grams], representing a dramatic increase from their initial 0.0164-gram mass at birth. This metric, measured under standard metabolic conditions at 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C], highlights the rapid growth phase supported by the mother's intensive milk production.

Adults of the species show notable variation in body mass, although most individuals in the population converge on a typical adult size. Field studies report that the ultimate wet weight, the maximum adult body mass attained during the life cycle, is approximately 40 grams [Wwi = approximately 40 grams], with a documented range extending from 16 to 44 grams in healthy individuals. This body mass is modest compared to many other dasyurids, reflecting an ecological niche focused on small invertebrate prey. Gestation itself is remarkably brief, a pattern typical for small marsupials, lasting only 30 days [tg = 30 days] at a maternal body temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]; this short in utero duration underscores the reliance on pouch development rather than an extended gestation period. The time from birth until the young achieve nutritional independence (106 days) represents the main window for maternal investment, with the post-weaning period beginning after this interval.

Sexual maturation in the brown antechinus follows a protracted developmental timeline, despite the species' short overall life span. Puberty, the attainment of reproductive capability, is reached at 285 days after birth [tp = 285 days after birth] under the normal thermal regime of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. This timing is critical, as it aligns the first oestrus in females with the highly synchronized winter breeding season. The males, similarly reaching maturity at this age, do not breed in their first year but instead delay their reproductive activity until their second year, resulting in a single, devastatingly synchronized rut. The maximum lifespan in the wild, at approximately 5.4 years [am = approximately 5.4 years], is an extreme value that belies the stark male die-off at a temperature of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C]. Males rarely survive beyond 11.5 months, placing this species at the fast end of the dasyurid life-history continuum, with a documented thermal baseline of 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C].

The ecological implications of this semelparous strategy are profound, shaping the species' population dynamics and responses to environmental stress. Because males invest all their resources into a single, intense mating effort, they become highly susceptible to stress-induced pathologies, including gastric ulceration and immune suppression, leading to their complete die-off. The annual reproductive rate reaches 7 pups per year [Ri = 7 pups per year], a figure that governs population turnover. The brief gestation period of 30 days [tg = 30 days] and the 106-day weaning period mean that the entire breeding cycle is constrained within a narrow seasonal window, particularly at 35.1 °C [T = 35.1 °C] — the temperature at which these critical milestones are recorded. Life history comparisons with other small dasyurids, such as the genus Sminthopsis, reveal that Antechinus stuartii occupies an extreme position on the slow-fast continuum, balancing a high metabolic cost of reproduction with a short-lived adult phase. Future research should focus on how rising ambient temperatures might perturb the energetic balance that governs these critical life history events.
